changes.adapted_text: We build the solution one scale at a time. Each new oscillation is supported in a ball about the origin whose radius shrinks with the step. Its velocity is initially small, but its short wavelength allows a large velocity gradient. The gradient from the preceding scales amplifies this oscillation until its own gradient can amplify the next one. The successive growth intervals fit into a finite time. This multiscale construction follows the approach of Córdoba and Martínez-Zoroa for the Euler equations with forcing \[[18](#cite-CMZForcedEuler), Section 1.2\] and for forced IPM \[[19](#cite-CMZForcedIPM), Sections 1.2.1–1.2.4\]. Córdoba, Martínez-Zoroa and Zheng \[[17](#cite-CMZUnforcedEuler), Theorem 2\] used a cascade of vorticity layers to obtain blow-up for the unforced Euler equations on $\mathbb R^3$ from $C^{1,\alpha}$ data smooth away from the origin. Related constructions give blow-up with forcing for the inviscid Boussinesq equations \[[20](#cite-CLMZForcedBoussinesq), Theorem 1\], the variable-density Euler equations \[[21](#cite-CLMZNonhomogeneousEuler), Theorem 1\] and the hypodissipative Navier–Stokes equations \[[22](#cite-CMZHypodissipativeNS), Theorem 1\]. Our companion papers proving singularity formation for forced IPM \[[3](#cite-AlpogeBuckmasterCoiculescuIPM), Theorem 2.1\], the forced Boussinesq equations \[[1](#cite-AlpogeBuckmasterBoussinesq), Theorem 1.1\], and the forced Euler equations \[[2](#cite-AlpogeBuckmasterForcedEuler), Theorem 1.1\] use forces smooth in space and time up to the singular time. In the present construction we use Craik–Criminale waves as building blocks and choose the initial velocity at each step so that the limiting solution is unforced.

changes.adapted_text: We first describe the wave construction of Craik and Criminale \[[12](#cite-CraikCriminale), Section 2, equations (2.4)–(2.10)\]. Let $D(t)$ be a smooth matrix with $\operatorname{tr}D=0$ and $D'+D^2$ symmetric. These conditions ensure that $U(t,x)=D(t)x$, linear in space, solves the Euler equations on $\mathbb R^3$, with pressure $p_D(t,x)=-x\cdot(D'+D^2)x/2$. We add to this linear background a velocity $$w(t,x)=\mathbf a(t)F(k(t)\cdot x),\qquad \mathbf a\cdot k=0,$$ where $F$ is smooth, odd and $1$-periodic, for instance $F(s)=\sin(2\pi s)$. At a fixed time, the wave has the same velocity everywhere on each plane $k\cdot x=s$. The nonzero vector $k$ is normal to these planes. A displacement of $1/|k|$ in direction $k/|k|$ advances the phase by one period, so $|k|$ measures spatial frequency. The amplitude vector $\mathbf a$ is tangent to the phase planes. The signed factor $F(s)$ gives the velocity on each plane, with maximum speed $|\mathbf a|\|F\|_\infty$.
changes.authors_text: We first describe the wave construction of Craik and Criminale \[[12](#cite-CraikCriminale)\]. Let $D(t)$ be a smooth matrix with $\operatorname{tr}D=0$ and $D'+D^2$ symmetric. These conditions ensure that $U(t,x)=D(t)x$, linear in space, solves the Euler equations on $\mathbb R^3$, with pressure $p_D(t,x)=-x\cdot(D'+D^2)x/2$. We add to this linear background a velocity $$w(t,x)=\mathbf a(t)F(k(t)\cdot x),\qquad \mathbf a\cdot k=0,$$ where $k(t)\ne0$ is the wave vector, $\mathbf a(t)$ is the amplitude vector, and $F$ is a smooth odd $1$-periodic profile of the scalar phase $s$. For example, one may take $F(s)=\sin(2\pi s)$. The vector $\mathbf a$ records both size and direction: the velocity amplitude is $|\mathbf a|\|F\|_\infty$, and $\mathbf a/|\mathbf a|$ is its unit direction when $\mathbf a\ne0$. The unit wave vector is $k/|k|$. Since $F$ has period one, $w$ is periodic in the direction of $k$ with period $1/|k|$, so $|k|$ is the spatial frequency of the wave.

changes.adapted_text: The affine wave lives on $\mathbb R^3$. To use it on the torus we first multiply its profile by a smooth cutoff in the particle labels. The cutoff vanishes near the faces of a fundamental cell, so copies of the localized wave fit together smoothly on opposite faces for any initial wave vector, including nonintegral ones. The preceding periodic velocity transports both the phase and the cutoff. For this transport of phase in geometric optics see \[[37](#cite-LifschitzHameiri1991), Section II, equations (7), (9) and (17)\] and \[[38](#cite-FriedlanderVishik1991), equations (5)–(7)\]. For the broader theory of asymptotic waves, see the foundational work of Lax \[[39](#cite-Lax1957)\] and Choquet-Bruhat’s construction near a given solution of a quasilinear system \[[40](#cite-ChoquetBruhat1969), §§2–3, pp. 3–6\]. Spatial variation of the background and differentiation of the cutoff now leave errors. The corrections below reduce these errors at each step until they vanish in the limit.
changes.authors_text: Craik–Criminale waves on $\mathbb R^3$ provide a local model for amplification. For the periodic construction, we localize each wave by a smooth cutoff supported in the interior of a fundamental cell in Lagrangian coordinates. We extend the localized field periodically and transport its phase and cutoff by the preceding periodic velocity, as in geometric optics \[[37](#cite-LifschitzHameiri1991), [38](#cite-FriedlanderVishik1991), [39](#cite-Lax1957), [40](#cite-ChoquetBruhat1969)\]. Since the cutoff vanishes near the cell boundary, the wave vector need not lie in $\mathbb Z^3$. Localization and the spatial variation of the background introduce errors, which the corrections below make small at each step and remove in the limit.

Once its frequencies have an upper bound, Bernstein’s inequality bounds spatial derivatives in terms of that frequency and the velocity norm. This is the role of mollification in convex integration \[[6](#cite-BDLSVOnsager), Section 2.4, Proposition 2.2\]. Write $U$ for the velocity left by the cutoff. Its Euler residual $R_U$ includes the small error from discarding the high frequencies (Subsection 5.7) and enters the next step.

We add the localized wave described in Subsection 1.1, using $F_h$ and a divergence correction. Let $X$ be the flow of $U$ from time zero, and fix a nonzero vector $k_*$. The phase $\theta$ of the localized wave is defined by $$\theta(t,X(t,a))=k_*\cdot a$$ for labels $a$ in the fundamental cell. A moving particle therefore keeps its initial phase, although the surfaces of constant phase deform with the flow. Their normal is $\kappa=\nabla_x\theta$, the local wave vector. For a linear flow this gives $\theta=\kappa\cdot x$, as in Subsection 1.1. After the first wave we choose $k_*$ so that, at activation, $\kappa=\lambda E_3$ at the origin. The spatial chain rule gives a derivative at fixed $s$ and a phase derivative with the large factor $\kappa$, both evaluated at $s=\theta(t,x)$. A wave after the first is multiplied by a cutoff $\widetilde\chi(t)$ in time that vanishes before its amplification interval; for the first wave $\widetilde\chi=1$. The derivative of the cutoff leaves an error of the size of the wave at the start of that interval, also carried to the next step.
